reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey offers the clearest measured figure for this sector. In the category it labels Other services, NAICS 81, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations, 15.0% of firms answered Yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The survey first asked the question in September 2023. That is the only hard adoption number in the material, and it covers a broader service category than nonprofits alone.

The sources describe what the sector does with the technology only in general terms. According to this site's own catalogue of ecosystem entities, the nonprofit and open source organizations it tracks steward models, standards, and shared infrastructure, and it names four verified organizations: LMSYS, which stewards Chatbot Arena as a shared evaluation platform for benchmarking model quality, Khan Academy as an end user of AI in education, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation, whose creative software AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The same page states plainly that the list contains no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, and that its notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

On the research side, the Center for Effective Philanthropy is described as examining how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, though the excerpt from its page shows only a headline about a participatory grantmaking model and does not report findings. The Nonprofit Technology Network runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and its page frames nonprofit technology as marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled for equitable use. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into learning environments where seniors and student volunteers explore practical AI tools, and it operates a global network providing standardized technical curricula to underrepresented communities. Candid is described as tracking grantmaking trends, including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure, and its page emphasizes that most grant funding and sometimes donations come with strings attached, and that recognition and media coverage do not guarantee a nonprofit's financial sustainability, which requires continued unrestricted support.

Stanford HAI provides the macro frame rather than sector-specific numbers. Its AI Index describes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind, and it notes that data transparency in the field is declining. The excerpt also mentions a reported sharp increase in AI adoption in medicine for clinical documentation, medical imaging, and diagnostic reasoning, which is outside this sector.

Money and vendor concentration are not quantified anywhere in this material. No source here reports nonprofit AI spending, vendor market share, or return on investment figures, and the catalogue page explicitly declines to confirm funding scale or compute access for the organizations it lists. What the sources do support is a capacity story: Candid points to restricted funding and evaluation pressure, NTEN points to inequity in technology use, and the equity project points to training and access gaps, which together suggest the constraint on adoption is governance and skills capacity rather than tool availability. The regulatory posture is likewise thin. Stanford HAI notes that governance and evaluation frameworks lag capability and that it is collaborating on a project about AI-relevant regulatory frameworks to improve predictability and legal certainty for providers and users, but no source here describes nonprofit-specific rules.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest, evidence-based read. Measured adoption in the nonprofit-heavy service category sits at 15.0% per the Census Bureau, so this is not yet a sector where AI use is the norm. The documented activity clusters around shared evaluation infrastructure, education, creative tooling, and community training rather than large-scale operational deployment, and the recurring themes across CEP, NTEN, Candid, and the AI Equity Project are funding constraints, equity of access, and evaluation burden. Where the sources are silent, on spending, vendors, and returns, a decision has to rest on the organization's own capacity rather than on sector benchmarks that do not appear here.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index at Stanford HAI describes its mission as supplying unbiased, globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public, tracking and visualising data on the field. This year's edition, the page says, shows a widening gap between what AI can do and our readiness to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while governance and evaluation frameworks lag. The page states that previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It describes the programme as an independent Stanford HAI initiative led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, and notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez on regulatory frameworks.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four verified organisations in the nonprofit and open-source foundation space, split between two nonprofits and two open-source foundations whose work touches AI tooling and evaluation, though the page states none of them build compute or power infrastructure. It describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-focused entry, stewarding a shared evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, and notes that such neutral evaluation infrastructure sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being assessed. Khan Academy is characterised as an end-user rather than a producer of AI capability in education, while the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, their primary missions predating and not being defined by AI. The page also flags what the data omits: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-centre specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.
